speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO SLAUGHTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries. On March 20 the problem of the slaughter of harp seals was brought to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries. Could the minister indicate whether his department has made any investigation into the situation, and if so could he inform the house of any action taken by his department.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO SLAUGHTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question.
A rather involved reply is required, and I will be happy to give a more comprehensive reply when my estimates are being considered by the house. However, with the permission of the house I should like to say in reply that harp seals are a species of seal that spend most of their lives in international waters off the west coast of Greenland and, in migration, between this area and the east coast of Canada, where the young are born on the ice floes off Newfoundland, in the gulf of the St. Lawrence and off the east coast of Canada at about this time of year.
The Department of Fisheries took estimates of the populations of these seals, for conservation purposes, by aerial survey in 1950, 1951, 1955, 1959 and 1960. Another survey will be taken in the next few weeks, in the latter part of April and the early part of May, so that a more accurate and detailed estimate of the population of this seal species can be arrived at.
A meeting was held in Halifax on December 8, 1960, at which the scientists and
Inquiries of the Ministry departmental officials outlined to representatives of the Canadian industry the scientific data available and the conservation measures required to ensure a maximum annual sustainable yield. The industry recognized the need for additional regulations but expressed the hope that these could be brought into effect gradually in order not to cripple their operations.
A regulation. was passed requiring all Canadian sealing vessels to be licensed beginning in the 1961 season. Notes were sent to the governments of Norway, Denmark and France requesting that they confirm their earlier agreements regarding opening dates for sealing operations and that they give consideration to a proposed closing date of April 30. Norway considered this date too restrictive and suggested May 5 for the current season. Canada agreed to the Norwegian proposal for 1961 only.
I might add that this item is on the agenda for the next meeting of ICNAF, the international commission for the northwest Atlantic fisheries. I should also add that it has been observed this year for the first time that a Russian vessel has been sealing in the international waters off the east coast of Canada. Communications have been sent to the government of the U.S.S.R. requesting that they require their nationals to adhere to the general regulations.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it will be recalled that when this item was before the committee last evening I showed some concern regarding the procedures now being used under the Live Stock Pedigree Act to establish the registration of certain breeds of cows. It was my hope that without having to deal with the problem further the minister would give the committee the assurance that he would consider this case again, the only case of major importance that the government has ever used to establish a precedent under the Live Stock Pedigree Act by means of blood typing. I had hoped that the minister would consider the many new developments that have taken place as a result of the scientific advances in blood typing and allied fields, and that he would look into the problem that has been caused by the use of artificial insemination, particularly with respect to this type of case.
During the intervening hours the minister may have had an opportunity of looking into this matter. It is a long, technical, legal case, and I had hoped that he would give it consideration without my having to take the time to deal with it further. However, the minister has said that the case is settled as far as he is concerned and that he is not particularly interested in the developments that have taken place in the years following 1952, when this case was brought to the attention of the department. Therefore I

Supp ly-A gricuUure
believe it is necessary for me to outline what this case was about and the developments that have taken place since which give rise to the claim by the farmer in question and other farmers in the area that a review of the case should be made, particularly in the light of the new information that is available and which has been presented in the form of a brief to the Minister of Justice and in modified form to all members of the House of Commons so they may peruse it at their leisure.
This case simply started from a domestic quarrel. The earliest information I have goes back to May, 1952. I have here a copy of a family court order which reads in part as follows:
Enclosed please find copy of interim order 1048 against the above named man. which was confirmed by Judge Allan J. Fraser, on April 29, 1952, for the sum of $20 per month for one child. Case dismissed so far as Mrs. Howe is concerned.
The family court case concerned Gerald Rowe. I am informed that shortly after the disposition of the case the wife, who had failed to obtain redress and had been informed by her husband that she was not going to be given a divorce, made a statement to one of the officials of the department in which she charged a number of things. An investigation was then commenced by the Holstein-Friesian association and a further check was made by a field man under the direction of Dr. F. J. Leslie, the chief registration officer.
The support case was in May, 1952. In December of 1952 a report was received by Dr. Leslie, the chief registration officer, and in the report there is reference to the number of cattle and some apparent infractions of the Holstein-Friesian registration regulations. The report reads in part as follows:
I would refer you to the sentence beginning on line 20, page 2, "At the time the inventory was taken it was noted from Rowe's stable breeding book that 25 heifer and no bull calves were born in 1952." In the light of information received from Mr. Smith-
I believe Mr. Smith is a field man for the Holstein-Friesian association.
-this sentence should read, "At the time the inventory was taken it was noted from Rowe's stable breeding book that 32 heifer calves were born in the calendar year 1952, of which 27 have been registered."
There seems to be a great deal of difference between the first and second sentences. The first sentence was based on what the wife had said, namely that 28 calves were born and that they were all heifer calves. When the field man inspected the herd book at the farm and made an inventory he found this was not the case. The government was now involved, and in my opinion could see possibilities in

this case. There is reference to several other cases, and as to one of them it is said that page 3.A.4 should be disregarded in its entirety.
The next step in the case in question was the laying of charges under section 17 of the Live Stock Pedigree Act. Subsection 1 of section 17 reads in part as follows:
(1) Every person who
(a) Knowingly signs or presents, or causes or procures to be signed or presented, to the reporting officer of an association or to the person in charge of the Canadian national live stock records, any declaration or any application for registration or any transfer of ownership respecting any animal, containing any material false statement or representation-
In other words, for this section of the act to apply the crown must prove that the man knowingly signed a false declaration or knowingly made or caused to be made a false declaration. Incidentally, in this case there were five or six charges laid, only one of which was proceeded with, that involving one calf known as Mary Bess Supreme. This calf was born on May 8, 1951. The dam was reported by the farmer to be Lady Bess Rena Echo. The sire was reported to be Penvale Supreme. The registration numbers of the dam and sire were also given.
The calf in question was vaccinated under the federal-provincial brucellosis control program on January 26, 1952. Less than a year after the birth of this calf another calf was born on this farm, on March 8, 1952. That calf was known as Joyce Rag Apple Pet Echo. The sire was Bond Haven Rag Apple Marksman and the dam was Lady Bess Rena Echo. This calf was inoculated under the brucellosis control program on January 31, 1953.
The investigation took place in 1952, as a result of which charges were laid. The court case was heard in L'Orignal commencing on October 23 and continuing to November 18. The charge proceeded with was that Mr. Rowe knowingly signed an application for registration with the recording officer of the Holstein-Friesian association of Canada respecting Mary Bess Supreme, a female calf, containing a material false statement relating to the birth of the said Mary Bess Supreme, contrary to section 17(1) which I just quoted.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the evidence adduced by the government in pressing this charge was to the effect that this farmer had claimed the cow was serviced first on July 31, 1950. It was claimed by the artificial insemination unit, or their agents, that she received a second service on January 4, 1951. The farmer claimed the birth of the first calf took place on May 8, 1951. He also claimed and had registered for over a year and a half, when this case was heard, a second calf

from the same cow born on March 8, 1952. It seems to me that it would be quite a simple matter for the government to press charges in this case and conduct a blood test on both calves, because I assume they already have on record the blood type of the bull used in the first service. The government claimed it was impossible to get blood from the second bull because that bull was dead.
It seems to me that anyone who understands anything about cattle knows that the gestation period is nine months.
You told us all that last night.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, but perhaps many members were not here last night. Perhaps some hon. members knew this before, but certainly the officials of the court did not know it. If this cow had a calf from the first service the calf would have been born approximately on May 8, as indicated by the farmer on the registration certificate. If the cow had been bred a second time and the gestation period had started on January 4, 1951, then she could not possibly, by any stretch of the imagination, have had a second calf on March 8, 1952, because that calf would have been at least four or five months premature. If the cow, as the farmer claimed, was bred on July 31, 1950 and had a calf on May 8,
1951,	there would have been the normal barren period of two months when the calf was very young. The cow would have been bred again around July, 1951, and this breeding would have resulted in the second calf being born as the farmer claimed on March 8,
1952.
A great deal of talk took place during this court case. The evidence is very extensive and covers four very large volumes. I suggest the transcript is not very good reading, because it involves technicalities which I believe had no bearing on the case and certainly have no bearing on the case I wish to make here. However, if anyone is interested he could read it.
Now, Mr. Chairman, under the Live Stock Pedigree Act the crown should have sought to prove that the first calf, Mary Bess Supreme, was registered as being born on May 8, 1951; that the name of the dam and sire respectively were given as Lady Bess Rena Echo and Penvale Supreme; that this information was false and that Mary Bess Supreme was not the progeny of such a dam and sire and also that the cow, Lady Bess Rena Echo, did not give birth at all, thereby rendering the said farmer guilty of supplying a false registration.
This case, if it had been accepted on its merits, would have established the legality of blood testing as a recognized method of
Supp ly-A gricvXture
establishing the parentage of animals. However, Mr. Chairman, the court case got so many things mixed up in it, such as whether cows can or cannot be bred during the gestation period, whether or not the semen was from this particular bull, that I believe the two agencies with which the farmer dealt should be supervised by the federal government. The first agency was the artificial insemination unit which maintains the bulls for service, and the second would be the people who are doing the work and handling the semen. They must be under federal control in order that the federal government may be in a better position to establish that the semen used is from a particular bull.
I believe the government should recognize the fact that the second calf, the birth of which has never been questioned, could not possibly have been born on the date suggested if there had not been the first calf. This first calf could not have been born from the second service, yet the government did not question the existence of the second calf. They accept this as a legitimate birth from the parents claimed by the farmer, yet the government questions the first birth. This course results, logically, in making the second calf premature by three or four months. I do not know how stupid some of the officials of the department are, but they must be very silly to adopt this technical position and expect to get anywhere with it.
In so far as blood testing is concerned, I may say this is a very interesting field. It is a field in which officials of the government and private research organizations have done a great deal more in the development of blood factors relating to animals than has been done in this field in relation to humans. They are to be commended for this. I do not believe there is any official or any veterinarian who will disagree with me when I make the statement that it is impossible to prove the parentage of a calf if there are two unknowns. If the bull is definitely not known, the parentage can be proven if the factors appear which establish the dam. Then only the sire would be in question. If the factors relating to the sire indicate that he could have been the sire of this particular progeny, then you would have reason to believe that the mating of these two animals could have produced this particular product. If, on the other hand, the cow is not known, by a reverse method and by a negative approach you could prove it was possible that this calf could have been the result of this mating or you could prove that this calf could not possibly have been the result of this mating.
In this case, Mr. Chairman, the farmer said the calf belonged to the dam but made no

Supp ly-A griculture
claim that the calf belonged to the sire, because he was not in any position to know whether that sire had, in fact, produced the semen which the artificial insemination unit sent to him. He was in the position, therefore, of knowing only one of the parents. The department seems to have taken the attitude that if the artificial insemination unit said this particular semen came from this bull, then that was a known quantity and, therefore, this negative approach could be applied; it could be proven that this calf was not the result of that particular mating.
Now I should like to read some statements made by some people because they are very important. I have a letter written to Mr. Rowe from R. J. Humble, D.V.M., department of pathology and bacteriology. He is probably the foremost veterinarian in this field in Canada and has done a great deal of research. This is what he says:
In regard to your inquiry concerning whether it is possible to prove parentage in cattle, the information you received from the United States is entirely correct on this point. As I have explained in previous letters, we cannot prove parentage. All that it is possible to do with this test is to show that certain animals could not possibly be the parents. Thus by the process of elimination we can usually eliminate all the bulls in a given group as not being the sire which will then quite often, but not always, leave one bull which could well be the sire, since he would possess the necessary factors, but we cannot prove that he is the sire.
However, if it is possible to eliminate all of the bulls in a given group but one, then it might be reasonable to assume that the one remaining bull might be the sire if there was any chance that his semen could have been used to impregnate the cow.
This certainly does not indicate the falsity of the farmer's statement that this cow is the dam in question, if we do not know the particular bull-and at this particular insemination unit at the time they were using four or five bulls-without doing what Dr. Humble suggests should be done, namely eliminating all other bulls not only in this breed but other breeds. It should be noted in this case that the collection of semen that was made on that particular day in question was from two Holstein bulls. Only one of them was ever discussed and, so far as I know, no one in the court ever asked if the blood testing had been done on the second bull. Obviously it would not have been too hard to have mixed up the semen at the source, and if this had happened this would have been the answer to this particular case.
There are other people who have said that this cannot be proven. This is again from Dr. Humble:
You may be aware that the parentage test done here at the college does not prove parentage by positive identification but by a test of exclusion. That is, certain facts in each case must be known:

let us suppose that the problem is a question of determining which of two bulls is the sire of a calf. The facts of the case must prove that only the two bulls could possibly have bred the cow. Then by the parentage test, it may be possible to show that one of the bulls could not possibly have been the sire. Since there are only two bulls involved and the test has shown that it was impossible for one bull to be the sire, then by the process of elimination it would leave the other bull as being the sire provided it could be proved by other means that only the two bulls were involved. If three bulls were involved, then in order to solve the case, it would be necessary to eliminate two of the bulls and leave the third as the likely sire.
I think this is correct, Mr. Chairman. If it is correct, why did Dr. Leslie not blood test the second bull in the artificial insemination unit on that date? He did not do it for the simple reason that he was not interested in establishing an honest case. He was interested only in getting a conviction on information that was given to him from another source that had absolutely nothing to do with either the Holstein-Friesian Association or the Department of Agriculture. This is why it was not done. This is why Dr. Humble in his evidence proved as well that this case was not an honestly established case, that there was reasonable doubt and that as well he could have established the other side; and it was only by the application of the information he gave the lawyers in the manner in which they used it that they were able to prove that what they did, when it would have been just as easy to prove the opposite.
The University of Wisconsin also had something to say on that matter. In a letter from the department of genetics Mr. M. R. Irwin states as follows:
In order to make any appraisal whatever of the identity of a calf as belonging to particular parents it would be necessary to have samples of blood of the calf, of the dam and of the sire. Without having samples of all three it would be impossible to state that the calf could not have come from a particular mating. The evidence from the blood tests will tell only that a calf can be excluded as belonging to the particular parents, whereas if the blood type of the calf is such that it could have come from the proposed parents, there are other individuals also which could have been the parents of this calf. In other words, it is not possible to prove parents by the blood test, only to make an exclusion.
There are other sources of information that would indicate that this was so. For this reason I think the government or the department, if they wish to establish an honest case and at least convince me and I think a number of the other members who are concerned about the breeding of cattle, are going to have to exercise much better control over these two aspects that fall within the jurisdiction of the department. I refer to the artificial insemination units and the

testing of cattle where there is a dispute and this is used as a factor in the establishment of cases under this particular section of the livestock registration act. I wrote to a veterinarian whom I know and he had this to say about this particular case-

I was pointing out that on pages 34 and 35 of volume 2 of the evidence in this case Dr. Smiley says that he drew semen from Penvale Supreme on July 30, 1950, which was a Sunday. On that day semen was also drawn from another bull, Elle Cross Snowflake Triune. On page 36 the doctor goes on to mention the process by which this semen was drawn off, and left open and again it was respecfully submitted that this was a further occasion when the semen could have become mixed.
I was suggesting that if the department in this particular case had thought the matter out more carefully than they did, they would have been fair to the farmer by testing all the bulls that were involved. The department should have tested all the bulls that could have been involved in a very simple mix-up, because semen was drawn from two bulls on that particular day. I think the department had an obligation to do this and not only to obtain a conviction, because I do not think it should be the prime interest of the department to obtain a conviction. In all fairness they should have given the benefit of the doubt to the farmer, to the extent of at least testing the second bull that was being used in the unit.
If the department had done that they would possibly, by the exclusion method, have established that this second bull might have been the sire of this particular progeny. If this had happened-and it may well have happened-

there would have been a different result in this case. In any case, the farmer should never have been asked to prove the sire of this particular calf when he had used artificial insemination. When the farmer receives the service slip from the artificial insemination unit he has to take what is on that slip as being the source of the semen, and he has to accept the name appearing on that slip as the name of the bull which sired the calf he registered with the association. He has to do this because he has no way of telling where that semen came from or what bull it was. He obviously has to take the word of the artificial insemination unit in this connection,
When the doctor, during this case, proved that the mating of the dam and the sire in question could not have resulted in the birth of this particular calf, in my opinion all this meant was that one of the parents named in connection with that calf was not the proper one. I should think there would be as much question about the sire as there was about the dam, particularly when a mix-up can occur much more easily in that field than in any other.
I recently received a letter from a friend of mine who is a veterinarian. He had this to say:
In regards to the Rowe brief, it certainly looks as if he got the dirty end of the stick. Most insemination units now colour their semen so that these mistakes can't happen. If I were the judge and was confronted with such evidence and knowing how some of these technicians work, I would throw the case out.
In my opinion the cow could have definitely been pregnant and come into heat and be bred by a technician again. Only a great deal of training and experience enables you to tell if a cow is pregnant at five months with certainty. It is possible, although difficult, to pass an insemination tube through a gravid (pregnant) cervix without causing an abortion.
Human error could have caused a mix-up in the semen at any point along the line from collection to insertion.
The parental blood test is pretty accurate even with the 15 factors, let alone the 40, but if the semen was mixed this wouldn't apply.
Tlie fact that units colour their semen now indicates that there have been some admitted mistakes in the past. I personally know of some cases where the semen has been mixed not only by the technician but by the collector.
I hope this helps a bit. C. A. V. Barker of the college is world known on insemination work and evidently his testimony wasn't even considered, which alone would justify reopening of the case.
This veterinarian owns a large hospital; he is a technician and a highly qualified veterinarian. He points out that artificial insemination units now colour the semen that they use.
I could go on and point out that in this particular case we have further evidence in connection with certain cows on this particular farm. There are affidavits from five people. One declares that three Hereford calves were born of purebred Holstein cows

and were sold to Arthur E. Lalonde. There is a declaration from Arthur E. Lalonde stating that three Hereford calves were purchased from Gerald Rowe in the first week of December, 1953, and they were sucking Holstein cows at that time. There is also the declaration of Raymond Lalonde which corroborates the evidence of Arthur E. Lalonde. Then there is the declaration of Robert Lalonde, who is no relation to the other Lalonde, that a Hereford calf was born to a Holstein cow. There is also the declaration of Orville Rowe verifying what Robert Lalonde declared and adding that they were the same cows as were sold to Arthur E. Lalonde.
These things happen. They have happened in this case. I indicated last night that this artificial insemination unit and their technician bred a cow that had been dead a month, as a second service. The technicians are not all exact. This man points out that sometimes his wife looked after the slips and sometimes he did. Sometimes he did them that day and sometimes he did them other days. This case could not have resulted in the statement which appeared in the Holstein-Friesian paper, as follows:
For the first time in Canada and possibly in any country, result of a blood typing to prove parentage of an animal has been submitted to court and accepted as evidence. In this case it was accepted as proof that the heifer, Mary Bess Supreme, could not be the daughter of the cow, Lady Bess Rena Echo and the sire, Penvale Supreme, as claimed by Mr. Rowe.
In delivering his judgment, Magistrate Lalonde stated the prosecution had proved by two different methods, practically and scientifically, that the parentage of Mary Bess Supreme, as stated in the application for registration, was false.
That is not correct. This statement which appeared in the Holstein-Friesian magazine it not correct. They did not prove this. They could not prove this. It is an impossibility to prove it when there is too long notice. Dr. Humble has admitted that it cannot be proved. Only an exclusion can prove that certain bulls could not have been the parents of cattle. They could not prove in this case that certain bulls were not the sires, and the Holstein-Friesian association is stating something which is not true.
I have nothing but respect for the interests, the aims and the aspirations of the Holstein-Friesian association, but I am very surprised at some of the bookkeeping they do. I should like to refer to one instance, because the Holstein-Friesian association comes directly under this department. If there is any infraction the department has the right to take it over and administer it. This case was decided in February, 1954. In February, 1955 Mr. Rowe received this letter:
You are aware in accordance with our letter to you under date of June 2, 1954, that at a meeting

of the executive committee of the association, held in Toronto on May 26, 1954, you were expelled from membership in the association and your certificate of membership was cancelled.
The letter goes on to say just what is involved. That was on February 21, 1955, and it resulted from his expulsion on May 26, 1954. But on July 17, 1954 the association sent him a card over the signature of the secretary in which they said his dues were not paid. So he sent them a money order, and that money order was received on July 27, 1954. It was accepted by Mr. Clemons, the secretary of the Holstein-Friesian association, without a protest. In July, 1955 a second notice was sent, saying again that his dues were due and asking him to send in the money to become a member again. After that second letter had gone out they sent him a notice acknowledging receipt of his money order, and when the post office checked on it they found it was received by the same person and cashed by the same person with no protest. They also sent the same gentleman forms to fill in to have his cattle graded as an official member of that association. Yet in their letter they go on to say:
If you persist in spreading false information among the breeders and members of the association, claiming that you are still a member or that you have been reinstated, we shall have no alternative but to give further publicity in the Holstein-Friesian Journal to the fact that you have not been reinstated and that you are not a member of this association.
I trust you will see the good sense of avoiding this action by making no further unwarranted claims.
He paid his dues, and he received a receipt for those dues. Again, the second year, he paid his dues, and I suggest he was a member in good standing at the time this letter was written to him. The receipts here can be filed with the minister if he wishes so he may see that these statements are correct,
All I am saying is that the association, as well as everybody else, can make mistakes, and it seems to me that the farmer has a rough enough time in this country in up-breeding his stock and trying to better conditions for himself and for the industry generally without the department working against him. In my opinion this department should be working for the farmer rather than against him. I am happy to think that most departments of government, and certainly most of the divisions of the Department of Agriculture, are working for the benefit of the farmer. Sometimes they are slow, but usually they work for his benefit. However, in checking over this information as a result of the inquiries which have been made I find that all we have done is to assume that the farmer is guilty and that everybody else has been right.

I am suggesting that this case should be reviewed by the department itself in the light of further developments in scientific knowledge which have taken place. We should remember that back in 1952 artificial insemination was not used as widely as it is today, and in view of the many mistakes which have been made-the hundreds of mistakes which have been made-and the fact that semen from bulls is now being coloured in order to prevent mistakes which everybody admits have been made, is it not the fair thing to give this farmer a second chance and at least go back and check the second bull which was being used in the unit and check the second calf involved in this case? Both calf and cow are alive; in this respect we are no further away from the case than we were then. I think the department has an obligation to do this for its own satisfaction.
I should also like to suggest to the department that they take cognizance of some of the mistakes which have been made by the artificial insemination units by insuring that more training is given to some of the officials in the early stages. A better type of training should be given to some of the people who are doing this work at the present time. They have done this work on occasions without any training at all. Certainly this technician had less than no training, because he was trained by a man who had never done the work himself. Though he may have improved over the years his bookkeeping is still as sloppy, according to the last report, as it was in the case in question.
I think the department has an obligation to interest itself in this particular field. It might not be as important as western agriculture or some of the things which concern western producers but it seems to me the farmers in eastern Ontario are going to be watching very carefully to see whether the government is taking any interest in this. They will not be too impressed by the minister standing up and talking about the New party and what it stands for. Frankly, cows are not interested in the Conservative party; they are not interested in the New Party or in any other party. They, and the producers of these cattle, are interested in getting the best guarantee they can that the semen which they buy for the cattle they are producing comes from the bulls that they expect it is coming from. It is only on rare occasions that farmers meet with any question regarding a cow not being the mother of a calf, and certainly in this case when there are similarities in the markings of the cow and calf very little question can be raised.
Last night many hon. members laughed as though they did not believe there was any

importance attached to these similarities, and suggested that we remove such references from the back of the Holstein-Friesian registration cards. I suggest that they appear there for the purpose not only of identifying the cow but to establish similarities in certain lines. While it is true that a white cow bred to a black bull may not produce a calf the colour of the mother or the father, it is likely there will be a predominant colour of either the dam or sire in the calf. This is an important enough matter that the breeders of particular types of cattle have used it for purposes of identification over a great number of years. Unless the government is now suggesting a new method of identifying this particular type of cattle I think consideration should be given to the similarity in markings in this particular case.
I will not take advantage of the opportunity, which I think I have and would be justified in using, to conduct a filibuster on this matter. I will leave the decision to the Department of Agriculture, and if it corrects this situation I will have a great deal more respect for it than if the officials sit back and say to themselves that the case is closed and legally cannot be reopened; there is a conviction, and whether it is good or poor, let it remain.

It would then be a building on exhibition grounds, and I do not believe the minister has resolved the problem by stating that the building can only be on exhibition grounds.

All I can say
is that such a serious matter would have to be given the most careful consideration. These special grants are given to exhibitions for national agricultural reasons and when any digression from the general terms of reference is suggested it has to be given very careful consideration.

When we were discussing this matter last evening I made a statement with regard to hogs and eggs. In specific answer to the question asked by the hon. member, I should like to point out that during this calendar year the present hog price support and the present limit of 100 hogs are in effect but I hope that during the year I can resolve some of the difficulties I see and come up with a formula that will do a little better job in achieving what we have in mind. I should like to point out that, having regard to the way the trade operates, the difficulties in dealing with this matter are very great.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say something with respect to what the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska has said. I do not quite agree that we should increase the number of hogs. I think that the floor price should be increased to a more reasonable level because in my opinion $22.65 does not bear a reasonable comparison with the cost of production of hogs, particularly in Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes. When we limit the number of hogs on which deficiency payments can be drawn I think the price should be at level that will return to the producer at least his cost of production plus a reasonable profit. I think that is necessary if we are going to have any stability in the hog industry. If a limit of 100 hogs is going to get us into a surplus position, then in my opinion we should reduce it to a figure where we are going to keep production in line instead of increasing the limit.
I should like to say a word in connection with the increase in the premium on grade A hogs. I am quite pleased to see that the minister did increase it to $3. I am disappointed, however, that there has not been a greater increase. I think we should be capable of a little more foresight in our attempts to encourage producers across Canada to produce quality products. It is about five years 90205-6-224i
Supply-Agriculture
ago since I took part in a federation of agriculture meeting in Calgary at which the premium on grade A hogs was discussed. Views were expressed both pro and con, but the majority of the members felt the premium should be increased to $4 per hog. In view of the fact the majority in favour of this course was small, the resolution was never presented to the Department of Agriculture with the result that the advantage of this move has been lost for a number of years.
It must be quite apparent to everyone who looks at the results achieved by the $2 premium that we have increased the number of grade A hogs by only a little over 32 per cent. This is rather ridiculous when compared with the 80 per cent of grade A hogs being produced in Prince Edward Island, Denmark and Holland. We should be using our best efforts to find markets for livestock products in Britain instead of trying to find markets for grain. I never could understand why we sell our western feed grains to Holland and Denmark where they are fed to hogs, the production of which is subsidized by the government and which hogs eventually compete with our hogs in the British market. I believe the Danish product has captured the British market only by reason of the quality of that product. I know I was there a few years ago and a chap was showing me a handful of western barley which he was feeding to hogs which were sold on the British market. At the same time this chap was selling his own barley to the brewery.
It seems to me we have to produce a better quality product than we are at the present time if we are going to get a share of the export market. There is no reason why we cannot produce as good a product as is produced in Denmark or Holland and capture a share of that export market. I feel one factor is that it is more profitable to produce a grade B hog than it is to produce a grade A hog. I expect that I am no better feeder than a lot of people, but I have no trouble in producing 70 per cent to 75 per cent grade A hogs. When you realize that only about 32 per cent of the hogs produced across Canada are grade A, it is time to take a look at this situation to ascertain what we can do to encourage a better quality product which would enable us to cope with export demands.

25. Freight assistance on western feed grains,
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out to the Minister of Agriculture an irregularity existing in the Saguenay-Lake St. John area with regard to the movement of feed grain from western Canada.
I have here a table supplied by the board of transport commissioners for Canada. I note that for a distance of 228 miles, for instance, or the distance between Quebec and Chicoutimi, the subsidy is 43 cents. For a slightly longer distance, that is 262 miles, from Quebec to Amqui, the subsidy is 68 cents. In the case of Jonquiere, for a distance of 218 miles-which is comparable to Mont Joli located 217 miles from Quebec and where the subsidies are 68 cents in summer and 67 cents in winter-the subsidy is only 43 cents. Chambord, in the Roberval riding, with a distance of 176 miles, receives a 43 cent subsidy, while St. Fabien, with a distance of 179 miles, or 3 miles more, gets 68 cents in summer and 67 cents in winter. And what about St. Arsene, in the Roberval riding-this will be one of the last examples I shall give-for a distance of 199 miles, the subsidy is also 43 cents, while at Bic, for a distance of 189 miles, it is 68 cents in summer and 67 cents in winter.
I could give many more examples, but I do not want to bore the committee with this detailed information. I am asking the minister however-he does not have to answer me today-to have this matter looked into and to try to take appropriate action so that farmers of the four counties in my area will not be discriminated against, compared to other farmers in my province.
(Text):

I should like to say a word in connection with this particular item. During the past few years there has been some criticism in Ontario about the continuation of freight assistance on western feed grains. I would hope that the minister can make this a permanent policy because I think it is good legislation. I would not say it is a subsidy to eastern farmers because I have never felt that way about it. I think those of us who are feeding livestock realize that if the freight subsidy were added on to the price of the grain we buy it would be impossible to feed western grain.

In addition, I think this is a subsidy to the western farmer and I am very glad he gets that much extra for the grain he is producing. I believe the subsidy is a protection to our Ontario wheat and corn growers because I think it results in an increased price for the grain that is sold here in Canada. In any event, this is going to the farmer so I hope this subsidy will be continued.

I should like to say a word on this item. I disagree very strongly with the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat, and who reached a very strange economic conclusion to the effect that the subsidy on feed grains used in eastern Canada goes into the pockets of the people who produce the grain in western Canada. I think my position on this question over the years has been a bit more realistic than that taken by the hon. member, namely, that anything that is done to wipe out part of the freight costs of moving commodities from the prairies to eastern Canada cannot help but be of benefit to both the producer and the consumer.
I was surprised to read that there was some opposition in eastern Canada, or in Ontario, to the continuation of the freight assistance on western feed grains. I hope the minister can assure the committee that not only is the policy to be followed for the present year, but that it is the intention of the government to continue this policy I should like to see this policy placed in legislative form instead of being left in the uncertain form of an item that is placed in the estimates from time to time. There is no doubt about it that this is a subsidy which assists in the moving of feed grains to eastern feeders and results in a price lower than they would otherwise have to pay for the grain they receive.
I would suggest that this is a policy that is in the national interest and is one that should be continued. It brings about a more equal price as between the prices paid to producers and the prices that have to be paid by the livestock feeders in eastern Canada. This policy is the very opposite of the misdirected policy having to do with the removal of coarse grains or feed grains going to feed mills from the wheat board regulations. That was a bad move; it is a move that is unsupported in the prairies because it runs counter to the general principle of this particular measure which is to bring about a greater similarity in the prices received by the western grain producers and those that are paid by the feeders across this country.
I would ask from the minister some comments as to whether or not it is the intention of his department and the government

to continue the freight assistance policy which has now been in effect for many years.

I should like to bring my age old problem to the attention of the minister. I refer to the freight assistance problem. First, I should like to quote from the Canadian Wheat Board Act, section 2 (1) (c) which reads as follows:
(c) "designated area" means that area comprised by the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and those parts of the province of British Columbia known as the Peace river district and the Creston-Wynndel areas, and such other parts of the province of British Columbia and such parts of the province of Ontario-
And so on. This area to which I am referring specifically namely, the Creston-Wynndel area, has never been granted any concessions at all under our freight assistance policy. At the present time the federal government has spent approximately $2-|- million in the construction of our Pacific Great Eastern Railway wholly within the province of British Columbia; and we are asked as the taxpayers of British Columbia and the taxpayers of Canada to contribute our share toward the construction of this Pacific Great Eastern Railway which brings a great deal of the feed grain out of the Peace river area. The payment of freight assistance in the Peace river area has been in effect for a number of years especially into the Vancouver markets. In view of the fact that this is a government subsidized railway, both federally and provincially, we feel that our efforts on behalf of freight assistance should be extended to the Creston-Wynndel area.
It has been brought to my attention that relatives, especially those living in the Peace river area who have relatives in the Creston-Wynndel area, are able to ship grain to the coast at a much cheaper rate in view of the subsidy than that at which we are able to ship it from our area. This situation has practically eliminated the Creston-Wynndel valley from this market in Vancouver which is rightfully ours. I have been advised that the province of British Columbia is ready and waiting to restore to the Peace river area in British Columbia freight assistance if they were to be deprived in this area of the federal subsidies.
The action of the department does not appear to me to be logical nor does it appear to be consistent in the interpretation of the act. Just what logic is there in setting one part of British Columbia against another part of British Columbia in connection with freight assistance problems? This creates a geographical and economic barrier against one in favour of the other. No country can ever become unified by such action. In view of the fact that both areas are in British
Supply-Agriculture
Columbia, I cannot agree that one district should be given consideration on freight assistance and not another. At the present time there is a difference of $11.20 per ton feed grains shipped out of the Peace river area and those shipped out of the Creston valley.
Last year I spoke on this matter and I received the same argument from the department, namely that this area is not part of the grain producing area for the purpose of freight assistance. This does not appear to me to be a logical argument. We are both in the province of British Columbia. At that time I received from the then minister this reply as found at page 4257 of Hansard of May 26, 1960:
I merely point out that this is a situation in which there seems to be no completely logical answer. We are still looking at the matter. The whole question of the movement of grain and particularly of the movement of feeds is tied up with the inquiry being carried on at the present time in the agriculture committee. After their report is submitted we may make changes as far as the movement of grains and the subsidy on grains, particularly from the Peace river area, are concerned.
That answer was given nearly a year ago and I feel that by this time they should have completed their investigation which would bring the Creston-Wynndel area into this freight assistance category. I feel also that we should be given consideration so that we can enter this Vancouver market. The difference of $11.20 per ton is a little bit too much to allow us to compete with the Peace river area.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few comments on this estimate which has to do with freight assistance on western feed grains, by way of an answer to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) who once stated that farmers should buy their grain during the fall and store it.
I gave two examples for the purpose of establishing whether it would pay the farmers or the feed mill operators to buy in the fall or in the spring. This is what I have found.
If the grain had been bought in October to be used at a later date, it would first have to be delivered to Pembroke from the harbour of Prescott. The option at that time was 82 cents a bushel, with a margin of 13 cents and loading charges of 1.4 cents, making up a total of 96.4 cents per bushel, or $56.62 a ton. Subtracting from this price the subsidy of $5 per ton, we get a net price of $51.62. To this price must of course be added shipping charges between Prescott and Pembroke,

Supply-Agriculture
which amount to $4.60 per ton, plus the interest on the invested money and the storage charges, for a total of $60.06 a ton, f.o.b. Prescott, in October 1960.
Had the same grain been purchased for delivery in March 1961, it would have had to be bought on the basis of the May options, which, at the time, were at 78 cents, plus the spread of 1J cents. So if you convert this grain into tons, you find that the price is $46.62 plus a $13.20 spread, minus the $5 subsidy which applies in this case as in the other, which gives a net cost of $54.82.
This will answer the allegation of the Minister of Agriculture to the effect that grain dealers would profit by purchasing their grain and stocking up in the fall. In the case I have just mentioned-the minister can correct me if I am wrong, but I have tried to get the best figures available-I think I am right in saying that the farmer has no advantage in buying his wheat in the fall and storing it until it can be used in the spring.
I think we should look for other reasons to justify the shipment of feed grains to eastern ports in the fall, so as to avoid finding ourselves in the same situation as last fall, a situation which caused the prices of feed grains to rise, thus affecting the income of eastern farmers.
Now, coming back to the statements made a moment ago by the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue) and the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox (Mr. Milligan), I should like to refer briefly to the subsidies paid to western producers and farmers. I am not against such subsidies, as I am sure they are really needed by the western farmers, because I had the privilege of working on a western farm for a year-that was about 20 years ago

and I had occasion to familiarize myself with the thinking of those farmers. I learned something of their language, and I was able to appreciate their attitudes and courtesy.
However, I have made a calculation based on figures provided by the "Current Review of Agricultural Conditions in Canada", wherein it is stated that in 1960, the prairie provinces received an amount of $77 million, including, under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act-the payments being based on acreage-an amount of $42 million, and under the federal-provincial farm assistance schemes for unharvested grain and for western wheat producers, another $35 million, which makes a total of $77 million. The number of farmers in those three provinces, in 1956, was 232,000.

Thus an average of $340, in round figures, went to each western farmer. If we apply the same figures to eastern farmers, including those of Ontario, Quebec and the mari-times-and I am leaving out British Columbia -we find that if the government had given our 315,000 farmers the same subsidies as were given the prairies farmers, it would have meant a disbursement of $104 million so that eastern farmers, and Quebec farmers in particular, would have got an additional $340.
According to a statement made by the management of la cooperative federee, as published in Le Devoir of February 2, 1961, the average net farm income last year, that is in 1960, amounted to $1,475. If the eastern provinces had enjoyed the same benefits as the western provinces, the net income of our farmers would have been $1,800 instead of $1,475.
The minister and the western members might think I am being critical of a policy which is beneficial to western farmers. Not in the least. What I am trying to point out is that there are farmers too in eastern Canada, in the maritimes, in Ontario and in Quebec, and that they too deserve consideration. We will soon have an act on farm rehabilitation. I hope that it will do us more good than did the crop insurance enacted two years ago.
Mr. Chairman, those are the few remarks I wanted the minister to hear. I hope he will consider the representations made by eastern farmers. I would be glad if he came out to visit the eastern provinces, particularly the province of Quebec, if he will allow me to extend that invitation. I also take the liberty of telling him that I will provide him with a chance to talk to our farmers and to tell them of what he is planning on their behalf.

Mr. Chairman, I think I should say a few words on this issue of feed grain assistance. This assistance has been in effect for a good many years. Over those years I think that generally speaking, hon. members of all parties have supported it.
A debate is going on among farmers as to which particular group gets a subsidy out of this assistance. The western farmer stoutly maintains that the subsidy is to the eastern

farmer, and the eastern farmer maintains just as stoutly that the subsidy is to the western farmer.
I have noticed a growing amount of criticism of this assistance in both the west and the east. Eastern farmers are saying it should be taken off. These are the farmers who are growing wheat in Ontario. Western farmers who are anxious to build up a feed grain industry out west say that it should be taken off because it is subsidizing their competitors in the east.
I will immediately relieve the minds of hon. members of the committee by saying that thers is no intention on the part of the government to change the feed grain assistance system. We have this matter always under review, and at the present time I think it is doing much more good than harm to any particular group. I think that in connection with trying to set the eastern farmer against the western farmer we would all be well advised to remember that we are all Canadians and that eastern and western farming are complementary to each other.
As Minister of Agriculture I have taken great pains to point this out, not only in the house but across Canada. I have pointed out that there is no need at all for quarrels between the two groups. The difficulties in connection with trying to assist agriculture to receive a greater share of the national income are big enough as they are, without starting a fight between the two different groups.
I think that with a little thought hon. members will find there are very few cases of serious clash between eastern and western farmers. If anyone tries to divide up the help which the government has given, on a direct basis of the number of dollars that go into one particular area as compared with another, I think they would be doing a great injustice to agriculture.
A comment was made about freight rates in Quebec. The reason for the recent changes in the province of Quebec is the fact that the movement of western grain to eastern Canada has been based on rail rates. However, of recent years more and more of the feed grain moving to eastern Canada has gone by boat. Since the rates in Quebec are based primarily on Montreal, the subsidy has been equal to that applied to Montreal plus the local rate. When boats discharge their cargoes at Quebec city cheaper than they can be taken by rail, then obviously people in the area around Quebec have the benefit of a much lower rate. It is very confused and I suggest to hon. members from Quebec that they have a considerable advantage in connection with the grain that comes by water because the subsidy is no greater than the actual cost of moving it in.
Supply-Agriculture
In some places the difference is considerable. Chicoutimi is a case in point. We have tried to rectify this situation and bring rates into line, and these efforts have improved the situation. The same thing is happening in the maritime provinces. However, I would point out that this is a question of rate reductions; changes are made which we think, in the first instance, improve the situation, but, immediately, we receive representations from other places asking that adjustments be made. I can say, sincerely, that this matter is under constant review. It is under very active review, because the representations we are receiving from the various groups are so contradictory in their nature. We shall do our best to eliminate the differential as much as possible.
I should like to say a word now to the hon. member for Kootenay East. I think the case he has made out during the last two or three years that an injustice is being done to the people who live in southern British Columbia has now been changed through the building of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway. I can promise him that shortly he will get an answer, yes or no, in the case of grain being moved into Alberta from the southern and eastern parts of British Columbia. (Translation):

I would like to thank the Minister of Agriculture for the information he gave me this afternoon and I hope that he will eventually find a solution to those problems.
I was a bit sorry to hear him say on a few occasions-and I have been listening to him for two or three months-that we are trying to pit the eastern farmers against their western counterparts.
I hope he does not take us for narrowminded individuals and that he does not pass judgment on us according to considerations I am not aware of.
We favour the western farmers as much as the eastern farmers, but we do want every farmer to have his share of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
Even though we come from Quebec, and whatever the minister may think, we are as truly Canadian as he is.
We have at heart the welfare of western farmers as much as that of eastern farmers.
Every time requests came from the west and estimates had to be adopted for the benefit of western farmers, I think we have never shown any reluctance to comply with those requests.
However, we would like the government, the Minister of Agriculture, as was indicated earlier by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) to go in the east,

Supply-Agriculture
to go in Quebec and see for himself that we are people like others, that we love our English-speaking compatriots as much as he loves them himself.
But, we also want our French-speaking compatriots to get their share of the national revenue.
I would not want to believe in the remarks he sometimes makes in this house because it would give me a poor opinion of his education and his broadness of mind.
As I say, to make us out as being against the western farmers and for the eastern farmers, I realize that may sound well in a debate and that it may be a popular statement in his constituency, but I do not think it is a right judgment to pass on the people of Quebec.
(Text):

I appreciate the statement the minister has made with regard to the seed grain subsidy and the fact that it is being continued. In stating that we should not try to divide the east and the west, the minister said that certain organizations both in eastern and western Canada have asked that this subsidy be removed. I should like to know from him what organizations in western Canada are campaigning for the removal of this feed grain subsidy. I am not aware of any organizations engaged in such a campaign and I should like the minister to tell me what organizations are involved because as far as I have been able to ascertain, the farmers of western Canada, certainly the grain farmers, are pleased that this policy is being continued. In their own minds, rightly or wrongly, they feel it is at least as much in the interests of the farmers and feeders of eastern Canada as it is in the interests of those who produce grain on the prairies.

I do not think there is any point in saying much about this. I have been making a tour of western farm organizations during the last two or three months and talking to various members of those organizations and discussing feed grain assistance with them. Several have remarked to me, mostly among the livestock associations, that as far as they are concerned they would not mind if it were cut off. I do not know of any organizations which have passed resolutions to this effect. I have simply pointed out that this feeling is growing. I do not think it is strong enough to warrant any action; I think it is just an expression of opinion that the subsidy is of no assistance to them.

I think the minister is engaging now in loose gossip, because he says that no farm organization has passed a resolution suggesting that this subsidy should be discontinued. Yet he comes into this committee and
[Mr. Brassard (Lapointe) .1
with the authority of the Minister of Agriculture he says that certain officials of livestock associations in western Canada have expressed to him the opinion that this subsidy should be removed. I think it is a disservice to agriculture generally to engage in this kind of idle talk and loose gossip. I have noticed a predisposition on the part of the minister in his policies to weight his policy against the ordinary grain producer on the prairies-
Oh.

That is what has been done. If some producer of high priced export livestock goes to the minister he seems to lend a much more sympathetic ear to him as witness the breaking down of the orderly system of marketing through the wheat board.
Nonsense.

The hon. member can catcall all he likes from the back. Those interruptions are his main contribution to debates in this chamber. But I would say this loose talk on the part of the minister, this gossiping of private conversations on to the record of this committee when no western farm organization has made any policy statement which is critical of the feed grain subsidies, should not be repeated.
I want to thank the hon. member for his gratuitous advice. We all know from long experience of the hon. gentleman who is the one who talks loosely and who gives misinformation to this committee.
No misinformation at all.

I did not interrupt the hon. member when he was speaking about me in such a loose fashion. I would like to point out that we have had a discussion spread over the last three or four months in the House of Commons concerning feed mills in western Canada, and I notice the hon. member said today in this committee that all the farm organizations in the west were supporting the stand he is taking. That is not true.
I said no such thing.

Read the record carefully and you will find you made a misstatement of facts today. I did not get up and criticize it because the hon. member makes a good many of those misstatements and it is difficult to stop them all. I am simply pointing out in regard to this ques* tion that I made a statement in this chamber which is true, and I do not like it very much when an hon. member whose record in keeping to facts in this house is not too good stands up and challenges it.

I never challenged the accuracy of the minister's statement at all. I did not say that he did not gossip with the officials. I did not question his statement regarding what certain officials had said to the effect that they might just as well take off the feed grain subsidy, but I did suggest that it was loose and irresponsible talk on the part of the minister when he related private conversations and statements, which he alleges have been made by unnamed officials, regarding a policy very much of interest to the agricultural industry in this country. It is difficult enough to maintain a good policy with the present minister in office without his trying to torpedo some of his own policies by this kind of loose and irresponsible talk, the accuracy of which I have not questioned at all. I have, however, questioned the propriety of the Minister of Agriculture in making this kind of statement when the organizations in question, in the words of the minister, have made no such policy statement whatsoever. The minister is merely referring to private conversations and is placing them on the record.

the second reading of Bill No. C-28, to provide for minimum wages for employees.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill has been before parliament on previous occasions. It was first introduced by Mr. Stanley Knowles who is now executive vice president of the Canadian Labour Congress and I have introduced a similar measure on several occasions. The bill would establish a minimum wage of $1.25 per hour for all employees under the jurisdiction of the federal government. A number of years ago it was considered throughout Canada that a basic rate of $1 per hour was a fairly good wage but because of increases in the cost of living and the upgrading in the standard of wages throughout industry generally over the years it seems to me that the government should establish a minimum wage not only for all those who are employed by it but also for all those employed in industries over which the federal government has jurisdiction.
Certainly it was made evident in Ottawa recently that it is necessary to establish a minimum wage law. Not long ago a number of convictions were obtained in the case of industries coming under the jurisdiction of the province of Ontario. With each application of the minimum wage law there is a growing indication of the need and desirability of establishing a fair and reasonable

minimum rate in those industries in which no organization bargains for the employees.
If the bill were passed it would not have any effect with respect to employees within industries over which the federal government has jurisdiction if those employees are receiving more than $1.25 an hour. The bill will not have the effect of reducing wages. It simply establishes a bare minimum and raises rates to that minimum in all cases where the federal government has jurisdiction. This would be a very simple law. It would be similar to laws that are in effect in all the provinces of Canada. The minimum rates vary from one province to another. The federal government, however, has depended upon prevailing rates, casual labour rates and other rates. We are now suggesting that a minimum rate of $1.25 per hour be established in those fields over which the federal government has jurisdiction.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate briefly in the debate on Bill No. C-28 having to do with the establishment of a minimum wage for employees of the government of Canada. As was indicated by the hon. member who introduced the bill, this is not the first time such a measure has been before the house. I regret to say that I was caught somewhat unaware. I had intended to speak at greater length on this matter on a previous occasion. However, I have hurriedly got together some of the material I had intended to use and I hope I can make a small but valuable contribution.
As a supporter of the government I do not hesitate for one moment to say that I support the bill now before us. We know very well that such a provision is basic in the establishment of living standards in our country and, so far as employees under the jurisdiction of the federal government are concerned, unquestionably parliament should give leadership by taking this step. Obviously the previous bill specified a lower hourly rate, but I think that is of no great consequence at this time. We all agree that the standard of living in our country is high, and I certainly believe this basic rate of pay would be required to maintain a family on accepted standards.
Back in 1935 the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, then prime minister, introduced legislation of this type in this House of Commons and carried it through to its conclusion. The Liberal government which followed referred this legislation to the supreme court and, of course, it was proclaimed ultra vires. Canada had agreed at an international convention to establish certain labour standards, including 90205-6-2251
Industrial Relations
minimum wages, and the country was therefore obligated by treaty to put such legislation on the statute books. I would ask hon. members to bear in mind that this action was taken by the Conservative government of that day and contested by the subsequent Liberal regime. I am not saying that, in recent days, the thinking of the Liberal party has not changed in this regard.
We must realize that in so far as the subject matter of this bill is concerned, the jurisidc-tion of the federal government is limited mainly to the fields of transportation, communications, a few corporations under federal control, and the banks. Certainly I would say that in those fields there are certain categories that require the assistance that would be extended by the terms of this bill. We cannot really expect that other phases of the economy will carry on at a high standard if the federal government does not take responsibility in the fields over which it has jurisdiction.
There will probably be some objections to be considered before we consider the detailed terms of the bill. No doubt these objections can be overcome during the course of the discussion or they can be referred to the committee and ironed out at that time. One such objection might be the possibility that the implementation of the bill would involve the expenditure of public funds.
There is one particular aspect of this question that concerns me somewhat. It is not that I feel the terms of the bill are wrong, but perhaps we do not have sufficiently in mind, when we are trying to determine what is right or wrong internally in our country, the fact that the federal government should take the lead in this field and establish a rate at least equal to the highest provincial enactment. We should bear in mind the fact that we are setting the standard for other governments.
Recently the New York Times published a comparison of hourly rates for labour in which the Canadian rates appeared. I think this is an important aspect of the matter, especially when we are endeavouring to establish a basic rate such as this of $1.25 per hour. The article revealed that in Canada we have an average rate of $1.72 compared with $2.13 in the United States. In the United Kingdom the average hourly rate is 66 cents; in west Germany, 54 cents, and in France, 38 cents. I do not have before me the figures for Japan, but we know they would be much lower than these figures.
I should like to quote here the figures relating to income per capita in those countries

I have mentioned. I do have the figures relating to Japan in this regard. In Canada the average per capita income is $1,400; in Japan, it is $200.
