Mr. Speaker, I have not in any previous year spoken on this bill but it occurred to me that there was one point relating to it on which I should like to say a few words. I refer to the necessity for the bill itself. I would not want my remarks to be taken to apply generally to business men in this country. I will therefore make it plain when I say that some employers about whom I intend to talk are the reason for or give rise to the introduction of this bill. I cannot tell what the percentage is; I hope it is a very small number of employers. However, there are certainly some across the country here and there who will take advantage of a workman in any way they can, sometimes merely to increase their own profit. Some may be driven to taking an unfair advantage because of the desperate circumstances their business is in and they will try to use anybody whom they can use in order to save that business.
I have had a little bit of personal contact with that type of employer. What I am afraid of in a bill like this is that where you force the employer to pay a minimum wage, it may lead him to feel, "Well, the government has set this fair minimum wage and, if I give the employee this wage, that is all I need to give him". It might in some respects deter an employer who, in trying to satisfy his own conscience without such a law in force, might be a little bit more generous.
I can recall working for a firm just prior to the war. At that time in the province of Alberta the minimum wage was 33J cents per hour. There was an old faithful employee who had worked for that company since 1897. He had started as a teamster driving a wagon delivering their lumber. He had graduated to driving a truck for the company and at the time I knew him in 1940 he was driving the oldest truck in the firm.
Industrial Relations
At that time he had had 43 to 44 years of continuous service with the firm. He was distinguished from the other truck drivers in that he was not on an hourly wage but was on a monthly salary. His monthly salary worked out to exactly what the other truck drivers would get if they put in a few hours overtime in a week. The only difference was that he received his pay every month and I am afraid that he did the same amount of overtime every month.
I was shocked by the treatment of that man when I came back from overseas and checked to find that he was still there but had just that summer been taken ill for a while. At the end of two weeks the accountant took his cheque to the secretary of the firm for signing and the secretary said, "That is his holiday pay". The man still was not back at the end of another two weeks and the accountant made out another cheque and took it to the secretary of the company who said, "He has had his holiday pay. We owe him nothing". I am happy to say that the president of the firm stepped in and said, "This man will continue to get his cheque, no matter what happens".
When we stop to consider the attitude expressed by the secretary of the company toward this man who had been a faithful employee of the company for 50 years, we are inclined to feel that certainly we cannot be too zealous in our efforts to protect some of the workers from some of the employers.
I am sure that the vast majority of employers in this country are not at all alarmed at the thought of a bill like this being enacted. I think the wage scales across the country are probably substantially above the minimum set out in this bill. I am convinced that in most of those industries where the pay is not above this amount there are many sound economic reasons why they are not able to pay it.
This, of course, causes me a little difficulty in connection with the bill. Certainly we all wish to protect workers. In so far as we are able, we wish to ensure by legislation that these workers obtain at least a minimum living wage. We know they require some protection, but we also know that conditions in this country vary considerably from place to place. They vary considerably from industry to industry. The conditions under which people work even in one industry may vary considerably. There are various types of jobs and there are certainly different rates that industries can afford to pay. An across the board minimum wage as would be fixed by this bill would certainly have different effects, depending upon where the people are employed.

Industrial Relations
I suggest that when we look at the different conditions and standards, a single rate across the country for all industries and all purposes would give some workers absolutely no more protection than they now have. The natural laws of economics, supply of labour, economic conditions, health of the industry, and so on, in one area mean that we are not giving those particular working men any protection whatsoever.
There may be other areas where industry is trying to get started and is struggling along, where the cost of living may be generally much less and where the economic value of $1.25 per hour would certainly be out of all proportion to its value in another area.
I would suggest that this argument is quite realistic, and as evidence of this we have only to consider what is being done by the provinces across the country in their minimum wage laws. I am not familiar with all the regulations and rates, but I do know they vary with regard to the minimum wage rate all the way from perhaps 35 cents an hour in some places for female help, to perhaps a minimum of $1 in other areas-it may be even more-for male help, depending on the job.
I note that this bill deals with more than just the minimum hourly rate. There are other benefits that this bill endeavours to provide. But looking at the provincial legislation-and much of it is of long standing-it seems to me that we would be attacking this problem in a much more realistic way if there were a little more flexibility in this bill.
I cannot pretend to come up with a formula at this time as to how the minimum wage should be fixed for any particular part of the country or any particular industry, other than by reference to provincial legislation. These provincial bodies and labour boards which operate in the provinces are constantly in touch with all the factors that affect rates of pay and the economic situation in their areas. Over the years they have evolved rules, regulations and rates and have set minimum rates of pay for various industries and various sections, taking into account all these factors. We might not be remiss in taking advantage of the work they have done in order to establish our own minimum wage regulations.
I should think that instead of fixing the rate of $1.25 an hour across the country- which, as I have pointed out, might not be too satisfactory for some reasons-it would be better to pass a bill to tie in a minimum wage rate which would rise, fall or vary according to the provincial minimum wage laws prevailing in the area or industry where these people are affected. Then we would be a little more realistic in our approach to the problem.

As the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) pointed out, when he first introduced this bill the rate was $1 per hour and now it is $1.25 because the cost of living and wages have gone up. I have no doubt that over the next few years, if this bill were put into effect, there would from time to time be amendments to increase that rate as economic conditions changed in the country.
If we fix a single rate across the country, paying no attention to the varied economic difficulties which have to be faced, I think it would not be satisfactory now, we probably would not find it satisfactory in the future and amendments would be necessary. I think we would have to bring in more than one figure if we attempted to cover the whole country.
Therefore, my first suggestion in connection with this bill is that we should take advantage of the work, time and money spent by the provinces. We should take advantage of their experience in this field and should make some use of the knowledge and figures they have compiled and the regulations they have evolved.
Let us put this bill, not on the basis of a rate of $1.25 per hour but on a rate which would bear a relationship to the minimum wage laws which are in force in the provinces for the particular area and the type of work being done. We should tie this rate closely to the provincial scheme.
I should point out that I am not advocating that it has to be the same rate of pay as is laid down by the minimum wage laws in the provinces. I am sure that if we looked at the rates now prevailing in some of the provinces most of us would probably be more interested in our own province and would feel a little dissatisfaction with the provincial legislation and consider that it has lagged a little. We would probably think it is time these minimum rates should be raised so that they are more in keeping with modern times.
When I say that we should take advantage of provincial legislation and experience, I am not saying that we should let the provinces set our rate. However, I do say that those factors which have caused the rates to vary from province to province, and in some cases to vary within the province, will probably be good reasons why our rate should vary also, I would suggest, therefore, that our rate should be an amount which varies, as the provincial rates vary, but should not necessarily be the same sum. It could be a percentage; it could be 1| times the minimum prescribed by the province; it could be 10 per cent more, or 100 per cent more, depending on the area under consideration.

I agree that we should give leadership to this extent. I do not think the federal legislation should set a rate which is less than that set by the provinces. However, I do feel that the most sensible rate, and the one which will provide the best protection for workers, is one that takes advantage of the experience which has been built up by the provinces.
There are a few cases where a minimum wage of $1.25 as set out would impose a hardship on the working man himself. These are individuals and merely because they are working people it does not mean they do not have their own defences, that they do not know their own minds or have to be led by the hand. I have seen examples of cases where a man might feel it is to his own best long term advantage to work for a very low wage at the start because he can see a new industry struggling to get going and believes that his own personal sacrifice will help that industry to get past its formative stage so that within a short time the company will possibly be able to pay him a wage much better than the minimum wage offered elsewhere in that area. A man might therefore want to join with his employer in making the sacrifices necessary so as to improve his position on a long term basis.
I have seen examples of employees who much prefer assistance of a very small guaranteed wage coupled with a share of the profits or bonuses and certainly this system does much for the incentive of the working man. Certainly those who are most vitally interested in the progress of the industry have their own welfare at heart. By setting a minimum wage too high we would make it difficult if not impossible for many of these worth while schemes to be put into effect.
I realize there are some employers who would take advantage of schemes of this sort, who would try to get their employees to work for little or nothing, and when I suggest that workers should be free to enter into such schemes I do so with the intimation that there is going to be some danger that they will suffer instead of gain. Having worked in the coal mines in the west, perhaps conditions there would be a good example of what I mean. I know that most of the miners who were digging coal wanted to be on a contract rate though some others preferred to be paid at so much per day. I have no hesitation in saying that those who worked on the contract rate worked about twice as hard as the other miners. The company man usually turned out to be the one who would do the least work, the last one you would choose to have as your partner if the two
Industrial Relations
of you were working in one place and were dependent on the total output for your daily wage.
I think this minimum wage is going to prevent a lot of ambitious hard-working people who are willing to make short term sacrifices in exchange for long term benefits from being able freely to exercise their choice. I think this will be more detrimental to them than exposing them to possible harsh practices by unscrupulous employers.
I do not like to deal with individual items in the bill but for the purpose of illustrating some of my remarks I cannot help but comment on the amount of money which it is proposed be deducted in respect of meals and lodging. I suggest it is most praiseworthy to make sure that a man is really protected where he is on a job where his meals and lodging are provided by the employer to make sure that the minimum wage provision is not circumvented by the charging of excessive rates for necessities. I suggest, however, that the rates for meals and lodgings must bear some relation to the actual cost of providing them.
We set in this bill a minimum wage rate of $1.25 an hour but we put the value of a night's lodging at 75 cents-that would be the bunk, the shelter and so on-and I think the price set for the meals is 50 cents. I find it hard to imagine how the same employer who must pay his cooks $1.25 an hour as a minimum, who must pay the most useless roustabout around the camp at least that sum in order to get the simplest tasks performed, must still be able to furnish food and lodging at those rates. I am not objecting to a working man getting those rates of pay but I think we have to be practical. We have still a lot of country to open up in Canada. In many of the places where people have to work the only way in which the project can be organized is for the employer to set up a camp. Nowadays wealthy companies with sufficient capital try to set up complete towns together with all the facilities, including facilities for recreation but there are still some areas where only a small development is to take place in charge of someone who possesses only a small amount of capital but large ambitions and lots of courage, the kind of person who originally opened up this country and who are still trying to open it up to the best of their ability. They do not have money for frills. They must be able to get in and provide some facilities for their employees. To put an artificial value on meals and lodging supplied-though these may have cost the employer three or four times as much-is going to make it correspondingly more difficult to get the project started at all.

Industrial Relations
I hope none of my remarks will be considered as indicating my opposition to the principle of the bill. I take it the principle of this bill is to protect the working man in his dealings with his employer no matter who or where he may be, to the extent that he will get at least a minimum living wage for his services. I am opposed to the flat rate being inserted because I think it would not do the job; it would not operate correctly; it would cause much trouble in some places and leave people without coverage in others. I would suggest that the rate be set at a percentage over and above the prevailing provincial rate in the area and that the item concerning food and lodging supplied need not necessarily be included if we have properly set out our prevailing wage rate.
There is nothing in this measure which takes into account the fact that we have in this country a good many people whom I might perhaps describe as difficult to employ. There is nothing in this bill that will encourage an employer to hire someone who is mentally deficient; individuals for whom we would like to encourage employers to find jobs in order that they might support themselves. This bill does not take into account the halt, the lame and the blind, and those individuals for whom we are attempting to find jobs. If jobs could be found for these individuals they would feel self-sufficient and would feel they were doing their part in this country. These are problems which I think can be worked out, and I would suggest to the mover of this bill that more progress could be made if amendments were included along the lines I have suggested.
Finally, I would say to the businessmen in this country that any remarks I have made about the hard-hearted businessmen apply only to a very few. I think the unscrupulous businessmen are a small minority. I feel most of our businessmen are hard-working honest individuals who give their employees the best treatment possible because they appreciate that their employees will in turn give them their best effort. I thank the hon. members for the patience they have shown.

This is a bill which I feel requires a good deal more discussion than we have had to the present time. I have spoken in regard to bills of this type on several occasions in the house and my opinion has not changed. There is, I feel, no hon. member in this house who is opposed to the principles of a bill of this type. However, I feel very strongly that the matter of minimum working rates is a provincial one. While this bill deals particularly with individuals working on federal government projects, there may be a very distinct clash with provincial acts causing a great deal of difficulty. The provinces in Canada have their own departments of labour, in most cases with advanced labour legislation. I feel that if this government supersedes that legislation without thorough discussion and the agreement of the provinces it would be entirely wrong.
For many years I was a member of a trade union and was connected with the enforcing of minimum wage rates in the province of Ontario, and I refer particularly to the industrial standard act. I am familiar with the problems involved in the enforcing of an act of this type. I feel that if this government were to move forward quickly in the passing of a bill of this kind without providing for an enforcement force it would get into serious trouble. The minimum of $1.25 per hour, as set forth in this bill, would be fair in an area such as Toronto but might create hardships in areas such as Newfoundland, Quebec and other areas. This is one reason why I feel that the minimum wage statutes should be matters with which the provincial governments should deal. I do feel that this bill requires a great deal more study before it is passed.
I had intended to deal with a number of other items but will say in summary that I endorse the bill in principle but feel that it must incorporate much more before it becomes a satisfactory formula for every part of Canada. For that reason I feel that it should be brought forward at some later date, perhaps in different form and at a time when all hon. members will have an opportunity to express their opinions. There is no doubt that it is a good bill but we should have the approval of the provinces before it is put into effect.

I am not sure whether this question is in order, though I may be subject to correction in that respect. If it is, I should like to say that at the present time we have no thought in mind concerning any change.
It seems that the words "at the present time" have caused some confusion among the public, judging from an article published in the Family Herald for April 13, 1961, under the signature of Jack Trower. I should just like to quote part of that article:
(Text):
It is doubtful, however, if Mr. Hamilton's very brief statement will completely satisfy the turkey industry. Answering a question in commons concerning the possible abolition of import quotas or United States turkeys, he replied simply that: "... at the present time we have no thought in mind concerning any change."
(Translation):
It seems that Canadian turkey producers, particularly in the province of Quebec, are concerned about this situation. I have received a number of letters from turkey producers in my area in this connection; they are concerned and they ask me to seek additional information.

(Text):

Mr. Chairman, I think the answer to the hon. member's question is yes. It does include all types of turkeys.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct another question to the minister. Has this maximum 4 million pound quota been in force throughout the year 1960?
(Text):

The quota year is the calendar year. Therefore the quota is for 1961.
(Translation):

And now, Mr. Chairman, in view of the answers just given by the minister, I must say that several of the letters I have received mention the fact that in 1960 over 6 J million pounds were imported from the United States.
On the other hand, in reply to a question put by my colleague for Drummond-Artha-baska, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Morris) replied, as found on page 2294 of Hansard, that in 1960 the importation of 4,444,298 pounds of turkeys, live or killed, not reported elsewhere, was authorized, under 77 permits.
On the other hand, if we examine the report issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce, entitled "Trade of Canada Imports, December 1960" for the 12-month period ending December 1960, and most particularly page 46, we will note that 4,682,777 pounds were imported under those 77 permits, I presume. The same information may be found under item 2261, "Turkeys NOP". Under another item, i.e. number 2013 of the same publication, it is noted that the importation of baby chicks and turkey poults reached 7,614,095 pounds.
I do not have the details of this item; I do not know whether there are any, and the minister may be able to throw some light on that subject. In any case, this item covers chickens, young chickens and young turkeys: 7 million pounds of them. Supposing that even a third of this 7 million were comprised of young turkeys, I feel that the figure of 6J million pounds which was given was not exaggerated.
Therefore, I ask the Minister of Agriculture why when a maximum quota is set at 4 million pounds, the importation of 4,682,777 pounds of small or large turkeys is permitted, including, I imagine, some 2 million pounds of young turkeys?
Does the department take the necessary steps to ensure that importers will not exceed the quotas permitted under their permits,

which quotas are intended for the protection of our turkey and young turkey industry? (Text):

I think the answer to the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, is that the Department of Trade and Commerce compiles figures relating to all turkey imports, whereas our figures deal with turkeys for consumption only. In other words, the trade and commerce figure would include poults that come in for feeding purposes. They are not for consumption.
Is the minister saying that turkeys for consumption did not exceed the 4 million quota?

I have not the final figures before me. However, if my memory serves me correctly the final figure was about 4,100,000. A check is made each quarter and the imports cannot go over 2 million for any one quarter with a maximum of 4 million for the year. However, if you get within round numbers of that figure, that is as close as you can get.
Coming back to the article I just read from the Family Herald, the concern of the turkey growers is that the quota will remain. Can the minister say firmly now that the four million quota will stay?
The answer to the hon. member's question is yes, the quota will stay at four million for this year and there will be the tariff of five cents.
I believe the Minister of Agriculture was one of the ministers who met with the members of the new United States administration. Was this one of the subjects discussed then?

There were a number of subjects discussed between the six United States ministers and the four Canadian ministers, on which there have been discussions over the past years. I do not know whether or not this one was actually discussed by itself, but the whole general problem was discussed.
Does the board of grain commissioners come under this particular vote?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No, it is under vote 29.

Item agreed to.
Board of grain commissioners (Canada Grain Act)-
29. Administration, $166,215.

I should like to say a word in connection with this vote. I certainly agree that the board of grain commissioners is doing a very good job in the marketing of grain. I feel this is an example of orderly marketing that has proven itself. I only wish we could

adopt this system of marketing for a lot of other products, and then agriculture would not be in the awkward position in which it is at the present time. I certainly believe we should be doing everything possible to protect the operations of the wheat board.
I am concerned about the restrictions that were lifted from feed mills in western Canada in relation to the buying of grain from the wheat board. I feel I should mention this item in particular because I was one of the people who took part in the negotiations which led to oats and barley being placed under the wheat board. The farmers of western Canada, through their farm organization representatives, came down to a meeting of the federation of agriculture and asked support from eastern Canada to have oats and barley placed under the wheat board. We thought this was good business. We thought it was a step in the right direction toward orderly marketing. At the same time, we realized the result would be an increase in the cost of feed in eastern Canada. However, we were prepared to meet our obligations.
There was no opportunity last fall during the meetings of the agriculture committee for the eastern organizations to present briefs on this subject. These organizations did not know anything about the hearings that were being held. Since that time I have received communications from the co-operative fede-ree" in Quebec, the maritime feed services in the maritimes, from the united co-operative in Ontario and the Ontario federation concerning this move to allow feed mills to buy grain directly from the farmers. I am concerned about this procedure because I think it represents the thin edge of the wedge which may be driven in to weaken the operations of the wheat board. I hope the minister will take a new look at this situation when the authorization expires in July. I think there is discrimination against our eastern feeders.
In addition, there is a principle involved. Oats and barley were put under the wheat board about 1949, and after 12 years the western boys are the ones who come down here and ask to be released from the wheat board restrictions. We in the east are still obligated to pay wheat board prices.
They were not speaking for the farmers.
I am buying western oats and I am paying $1 a bushel.
That is a crime.

I was looking at the wheat board quotations and they are paying 78J cents for oats. The minister was kind enough

to give us the figures to show what the feed mills were paying the farmers for western grain. In going over this list I find that none of the mills was paying over 55 cents for oats, 65 cents for barley and 95 cents for wheat. Certainly, if I could buy grain at those prices I would feel I could very easily beat the market. After going over these prices, I find they are the initial prices the wheat board is paying the farmer for grain. As I understand it, there is always a payment made to the farmers after the crop has been sold. I do not want to see the western farmer faced with any more problems or expense, but it does seem too bad that he cannot buy his grain as he would like.
I feel we should tie down the feed mills so that they would at least pay the initial price paid by the wheat board. I understand there are freight charges, elevator storage and all the rest of it placed against this grain when it is bought by the feed mills in western Canada. There could be regulations imposed upon the feed mills so that when they buy directly from the farmers they must pay the initial price paid by the wheat board plus whatever return there is from the grain after the crop is sold, on the same basis as we pay in the east.
This is not something new. I have discussed this grain question for the last 15 years in farm organizations. I have been told we need not pay these exorbitant prices for grain. We can buy it directly from the wheat board and store it, and that is exactly what the western farmer can do. Instead of buying from the feed mills, he can buy from the wheat board, store it and then take it over to the feed mill for processing. We have been told for five years that we are being exploited because, as I understand it, there are no storage facilities down here for the grain.
I have been told that the elevator storage at Prescott and Kingston at the present time is filled with export wheat No. 3 which has been there for some three or four years, with the result that there is no room for any more grain to be placed in those elevators. As a consequence we are left to be exploited by the grain trade. I think that is one of the reasons why we pay such enormous prices for grain today as compared with what the western farmer gets. I would not mind paying $1 a bushel for oats if the western farmer were getting that price on the farm, but I know he is not getting it.
For three years many of us have asked for the closing of the grain exchange because of the speculative market. We are leaving it wide open for the speculators to take advantage of the western producer and also of the feeder in the east. That is exactly what
Supply-Agriculture
is taking place at the present time. We are left in short supply, with the result that we are obliged to depend on rail shipment. We are obliged to depend on the trade. They know we are in short supply and they exploit us and take advantage of the situation. I hope these conditions can be changed. I felt I should mention these things because I was one of the people who sat in at these negotiations. I think a principle is involved, namely the protection of the feeder in the east as well as the producer in the west. It seems to me that we must have one policy for agriculture right across Canada. Unless we have that kind of policy I do not think justice can be done to the feeders in eastern Canada.

I rise on a point of order for purposes of clarification owing to the fact that this year we have, I think for the first time, the transfer of responsibility for the Canadian wheat board to the Minister of Agriculture, the Canadian wheat board having previously been under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and having been in his estimates. I have no quarrel with that transfer. However, I have spoken to the Minister of Agriculture and have pointed out to him that unless a member of the committee of supply speaks on item No. 1, he might have some difficulty in speaking on problems tremendous in their scope which involve the Canadian wheat board.
I do not think the Canada Grain Act or the jurisdiction of the board of grain commissioners perhaps permitted the discussion we had from my hon. friend from Prince Edward-Lennox. However, I certainly did not want to interrupt him because he is a very conscientious member of the House of Commons and a good friend of mine. Nevertheless with the transfer of responsibility from the Department of Trade and Commerce to the Department of Agriculture I think we should have, as members of parliament, some clarification from the minister as to what debate he would expect in the future.
In my conversation with him, I think he asked me to look up the former practice when the wheat board was under the Department of Trade and Commerce. I attempted to do so during the dinner hour but I could not find that the situation was any different. I could not find under the Department of Trade and Commerce an item, shall I say, that would be equivalent to the absence of an item here in agriculture. It is a very big area of the minister's responsibility, whether he be the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have no particular suggestion to make if this has been traditional. We always have room for change and improvement.

I have already spoken this session making some complaint with regard to dollar items which offer opportunity for debate but which may, in so far as the estimates are concerned, have no real meaning. In this case I think perhaps I should be consistent. Unknown as it sometimes is to some of those interested in agriculture in eastern Canada, the Canadian wheat board operation is an operation of western farmers; and from what we are doing tonight it is obvious that the Canadian wheat board and its western farmer members absorb the cost of operation. We as parliamentarians are therefore not called upon to vote money for the operation of the Canadian wheat board. However, I thought perhaps the new Minister of Agriculture might give this matter some thought because it is extremely important.
On the point of order which the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has raised, if I may,-

I asked the hon. member to excuse me.

I should like to suggest that the debate on this matter of where the wheat board should be discussed should be dealt with at this time. speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, my recollection is that in the session of 1957-58, the summer session of 1958 and the sessions of 1959 and 1960, when I was in charge of the wheat board, it was discussed under the first item of the Department of Trade and Commerce. That is my recollection of what has been done in the past. I have a good recollection of the debate last year on this matter. At that time quite considerable attention was paid to the Canadian wheat board, and that was done under the first item.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, if I may be allowed to say another word, under the former administration there was no hesitation in allowing discussion of the general grain situation when we came to a grain item. speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Have you the page references of Hansard to substantiate those statements?

No, I have not; but I have been here a long time and I make that statement knowing it to be correct.

I would make a further statement. I plead with the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who is the house leader, to look at this question rather leniently because the progress in this house for the session must depend upon the co-operation of all parties.
It was announced before the Easter recess that the first order of business for last Monday would be a supply motion. For reasons of the convenience of the government it was felt necessary to change the order of business. It is quite correct that the Minister of Veterans Affairs tried repeatedly to reach me in Saskatchewan and was unable to do so through no fault of his own. However, I think that since the hon. members of this house, including the members of this group, were prepared to give unanimous consent to the government to change the order of business and to take estimates on a day when hon. members had the right to move a supply motion, no matter what the agreement, it is only a fair request to ask that the very important item of Canadian wheat board policy should be open for discussion by hon. members under this item, or, as I suggested earlier, at the end of the detailed items, to allow us to revert to item 1 for a discussion on this particular matter.
There are one or two other specific matters which I should like to discuss, but I do not want to get into them at this time. However, surely the question of the Canadian wheat board policy is of sufficient importance that the government should accede to a request that an appropriate place be allocated, either at this moment or at some later stage by agreement, for discussing this policy.
Because of the visit of Prime Minister Macmillan and certain arrangements which the government had to make, those in the official opposition and in this group were co-operative and I suggest the government should also be co-operative with us on occasion.

Why did you say "on
occasion"? We are frequently co-operative.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I reply to the hon. member who was unavailable by telephone on Friday and who was expected to return, according to his office, on Sunday night-and had he returned then I would have been in touch with him in regard to the changes in the program for Monday-that

we are quite agreeable to making some reasonable arrangement with the hon. member for Assiniboia.
If we could complete the remaining few items under the Department of Agriculture I would suggest, in deference to the wish of the hon. member for Assiniboia who was unavoidably absent yesterday, that he be permitted to speak on this general subject if he wishes, leaving sufficient time for the Minister of Agriculture to reply.
If that is agreeable to other hon. members of the committee, I presume it will be agreeable to the Minister of Agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order, having raised this problem because it arises from a transfer of jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board, may I say that I had a short time for research during the dinner recess. I am informed very authoritatively that affairs relating to the Canadian wheat board have for many years been discussed under the item concerning the board of grain commissioners.
I would agree immediately with the suggestion of the leader of the house that we might postpone this item at the moment, if this is agreeable to the hon. member for Assiniboia, for an opportunity for us all to look at the traditional pattern and keep up the tradition.
I really raised the point because I thought we should have something more reliable to follow next year in our procedure. I thought that the Canadian wheat board was of sufficient importance that no hon. member of the committee should be under any misconception that he must speak with respect to the salary of the Minister of Agriculture or otherwise have no chance to speak at all. It was on that basis that I thought perhaps we could raise this problem.
I do not for a moment suggest that we should depart from our traditional practice, and I hope that is not the intention of the leader of the house. However, if it is acceptable to most hon. members of the committee I would suggest that we continue with other items and in the meantime we will have an opportunity to look at the pattern of debates in the past with respect to the Canadian wheat board to establish the precedents.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I trust that the leader of the house did not mean that the debate will be entirely between the leader of the C.C.F. group and the Minister of Agriculture. I hope the house leader meant that the opportunity would be open to all of us to take part in this debate.
Oh, quite.
I did not take that from What the minister said.

I am, of course, in the hands of the committee but I may point out that the advice I have been able to secure would indicate that this question of the wheat board should be discussed under item 1 of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, now that responsibility has been transferred to that department, in the same way as it was discussed in the past under item 1 of the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. speechtext: Will you finish the discussion tonight?

I will finish my part of the discussion tonight but I cannot be held responsible for what other hon. members may do. I will make my comments if I am given an opportunity. But I suggest to the leader of the house that if the government wants the co-operation of hon. members from all sides it should consider this question I am putting forward now because co-operation does work both ways and I think this is a reasonable request. Indeed, I am a little surprised there has been some hesitancy on the part of the government about granting it.

On the point of order, the leader of the house, the present Minister of Veterans Affairs, was formerly minister

of trade and commerce, and responsibility for the wheat board was then his. It has been transferred to the Minister of Agriculture, I think during the present session.
Now, to judge by the remarks made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs the hon. gentleman was just about as uncertain as I was with regard to some of the history behind this. I want to assure him that we in this party are not going to abuse unduly the privilege if a discussion of this item is permitted. I cannot, of course, give a guarantee for all my colleagues but it is not our intention to delay the passage of these estimates. However, I thought it was appropriate to raise the question when I noticed that we have really nothing specific in the estimates under which the wheat board could be discussed. I mentioned to the new Minister of Agriculture tonight that I did have some responsibility, having been associated with the former minister of finance. We did not do better then to provide such an item. We discussed this in a most friendly way. I suggested that there was something wrong if we did not seek to question the vote for the minister's own salary, that somewhere else in the book of estimates members should have no opportunity to discuss the activities of such an important quasi-governmental organization as the wheat board even if the wheat board charges all its costs to the farmers and does not ask the taxpayers for anything in this book of estimates.

In view of the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for Assiniboia I think I should make my personal attitude on this subject very clear. I welcome at all times a debate on the Canadian wheat board and its operations but I should like to make it very plain to the committee-and this is a matter of personal privilege which is now raised-that I have had my estimates before the committee on several days this year. On the night prior to Friday, March 24, for example, a decision or agreement was made that I would have the next day for my estimates, the whole Friday. I was asked to step aside for one speaker from the C.C.F. group, one speaker only who would take just half an hour. When the debate began on Friday morning the hon. member for Timmins spoke as was agreed and then he was followed by several C.C.F. speakers all of whom went against the agreement made with me with regard to my estimates.
I made no agreement with you.

I wish the hon. member for Assiniboia would let me finish. I understood that when the hon. member who speaks for that party comes across-and the

hon. member is present now-and says we have agreed that there should be just one speaker, the word of that member covers the word of all the other members. I think this question of understandings and convenience works both ways, and if this house is to operate as it ought to operate in a democratic parliament there has to be understanding on both sides. I think there has to be some very serious consideration given, Mr. Chairman, before we revert to an earlier item and open up this debate again.
The second point I should like to make is that the hon. member for Assiniboia has spoken on item 1. He has spoken on the wheat board. Now he is again asking for the same privilege. This was on March 24 and the understanding was reached the previous night.

Mr. Chairman, a short time ago the Minister of Agriculture raised the matter of a broken agreement in which I was supposed to have participated. Since then I have had an opportunity to check Hansard. I believe the minister referred to March 24. I find that the minister is mixing up two different debates.

I think the minister has mixed this up with the debate on NATO under the supplementary estimates, at which time there was an agreement entered into by myself and the rest of this party.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words on vote 29, the administration of the board of grain commissioners. I have some statistics here that I think are rather amazing in light of all the wild and optimistic statements which have been made by the Minister of Agriculture.
Our overseas clearances of barley to date have been only 13.2 million bushels, while a year ago they were 25.9 million bushels. This is a drop of 12.7 million bushels. The amount exported, the overseas clearances of barley this year to date, are just about 50 per cent of the amount last year.
One can only ask why we have such gloomy figures, in light of the minister's boast that everything is well, everything is improving and conditions are getting better. The grain situation in Canada today is probably tighter than it has ever been. There is probably more congestion than there has ever been. The farmers are having great difficulty in marketing grain because of the congestion. I do not see from the figures in my hand that there is any real hope that this congestion is going

Supply-Agriculture
to be alleviated, because month after month the congestion seems to get worse.
The visible supplies of all grains in various positions to date amount to 413.2 million bushels, whereas a year ago they amounted to 364.7 million bushels. I ask the minister whether this is a deliberate policy on the part of the government to take in every possible bushel of grain to bring about a further congestion, a further filling of available storage space, or whether these visible supplies of grain in all positions-
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order-
-has been increased because-

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. This item has to do with the administration of the board of grain commissioners. Our hon. friend from Assiniboia has been away for a few days and since he returned he has been trying very hard to crowd Hansard. I suggest that the hon. member is entirely out of order when he discusses visible supplies and export shipments of grain.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman may be an authority on the rules but he is scarcely an authority on the board of grain commissioners. The statistics that I have quoted have a very great deal to do with the administration of the board of grain commissioners. This is what the board of grain commissioners is all about.
My hon. friend may not know it, but the board of grain commissioners has to do with the assembling, the grading and storage of grain all across this country. The wheat board has to do with issuing tickets and it has to do with carrying out some of the government's policies like this dollar an acre payment, which is still treaty money. The Canadian wheat board has to do with the markets, or the lack of markets.
When it comes to the amount of congestion in the country and the kind of statistics to which I have referred, these matters certainly have to do with the board of grain commisioners. My honourable and learned friend, who is usually very much on the ball and very accurate in his frequent and consistent interruptions, is away off base tonight. The statistics to which I have referred have to do with the administration of the board of grain commissioners.
I want to ask the minister some more questions. Why should the visible supplies of grain be going up by such an amount and so fast? Has it to do with more storage facilities available in the country, or has it
[Mr. Argue.1
to do with the greater congestion that has been brought about by the policies of the government?
I want to know why, after all this tremendous fanfare about new markets, the market for overseas clearance of Canadian oats, should have just about disappeared? It was .8 million bushels of wheat this year, as compared with 3.8 million bushels of wheat to the same date a year ago. I think the minister owes it to the committee to tell us why these statistics are so gloomy, in light of his very optimistic statements to the House of Commons.
I want to know the reason for the figures concerning farmer's marketings to date, 199 million bushels of wheat as compared with 180.8 million bushels a year ago. I want to know why the situation as far as quotas in the minister's province and my own are concerned should be so bleak and so gloomy. I ask the Minister of Agriculture why he does not do something about the quotas.
I do not know why many of the farmers he and I represent should, after eight months of the crop year, be told to market only a one bushel quota, and some of them hoping to have a two bushel quota-

We used to ask the minister of trade commerce what the exports had been, and he would say, "Oh, I cannot disclose the exports of grain because that would put the wheat board in a difficult competitive position". It does. mess. I do not wonder why he cannot answer and tell us the reason for this tremendous congestion.

of order. It seems to me, sir, that it should not be forgotten that in past years, until an order was made by the governor in council, the board of grain commissioners and the wheat board were under the jurisdiction of the minister of trade and commerce. It does seem to me that all of us in this committee are taking a very dangerous position when we suggest that one of the most important of all the industries in this country should be precluded from discussion because of technicalities. I do not think that our conduct in this regard will be very well viewed in the country.

Mr. Chairman, I am continuing to point out how very difficult the grain situation is, and I suggest this is very much in order, since I shall be quoting from the board of grain commissioners statistics branch, not the wheat board statistics branch.
The Canadian grain position at the close of business, Wednesday, March 29, 1961 showed that Canadian visible wheat totalled 413.2 bushels reflecting a decline of only 1.2 million bushels during the week under review. Preliminary marketings were steady at 4.4 million bushels but export shipments fell off form the relatively high level in recent weeks to only 3.5 million bushels clear.
The minister may not like to hear this, and may say that it is the wheat board's policy, but I am quoting from a publication of the board of grain commissioners. It shows 1.5 million bushels from Vancouver and 2 million bushels from the east coast ports of Saint John and Halifax. This is a dismal and black showing which the Minister of Agriculture of course cannot defend. Clearings now total 29.9 bushels of wheat, some 5.6 bushels better than export wheat loadings from these two ports during the 1959-60 season.
The minister may take some encouragement from that last sentence but I suggest that these statements are serious and we should have a reply from the minister. He should tell us why, after he goes out across this country telling farmers that everything is well and that conditions are improving-just have faith in John and we will get out of the woods somehow-these statistics keep coming in showing the serious position of the grain trade in Canada at this time. I think our producers would like to know whether there are going to be additional facilities provided for the storage of grain; whether these statistics put out by the board of grain commissioners are likely to show any improvement in the weeks ahead or whether

there is going to be continued congestion and a further drop-off-I hope not-of export clearings and an almost total disappearance of the market for oats; a reduction in overseas clearances for barley of almost 50 per cent. The Minister of Agriculture apparently does not want to defend this position but I think he owes it to this committee to tell us what he intends to do about this difficult situation.
I would like to know whether the board of grain commissioners has anything to do at this time with the handling of box cars. In years gone by the allocation of box cars was done by one of the commissioners of the board, a Mr. Milner, who used his authority with railway	companies-or	persuasive
powers, when he had any-to try to arrive at an agreement in respect of the allocation of box cars. I would like to know the number of complaints the minister has received with regard to the grading of grain and dockage and overages. Clearly all of these questions are within the jurisdiction of the board of grain commissioners.
